title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This page (§§43–45 and the statement of Problem IV) continues Euler's programme of turning alternating series into equivalent continued fractions, whose convergents equal the partial sums of the series.

Theorem VI (previous page) states that the series s = 1/α − 1/(αβ) + 1/(αβγ) − … gives 1/s = α + α/(β−1 + β/(γ−1 + …)).

§43: Euler substitutes α→α/a, β→β/b, γ→γ/c, … so the series becomes s = a/α − ab/(αβ) + abc/(αβγ) − …. Theorem VI then gives 1/s = α/a + (α/a)/(β/b − 1 + (β/b)/(γ/c − 1 + …)). He multiplies both sides by a, then the first partial fraction top and bottom by b, the second by c, and so on. This is an equivalence transformation of the continued fraction.

§44 (Theorem VII): for s = a/α − ab/(αβ) + abc/(αβγ) − …, one has a/s = α + αb/(β − b + βc/(γ − c + γd/(δ − d + …))). This is Euler's classical series-to-continued-fraction formula with ratios of successive terms a/α, b/β, ….

§45, example:
- Take a,b,c,… = 1,3,5,7,… and α,β,γ,… = 2,4,6,8,….
- The series is s = 1/2 − 3/8 + 15/48 − …, i.e. 1 − (1+1)^{−1/2} from the binomial series, so s = 1 − 1/√2 = (√2−1)/√2.
- Every partial denominator β−b, γ−c, … equals 1, giving √2/(√2−1) = 2 + 2·3/(1 + 4·5/(1 + 6·7/(1 + …))).
- Subtracting 1 gives 1/(√2−1) = √2+1 = 1 + 2·3/(1 + 4·5/(1 + …)).
- Since √2 − 1 = 1/(√2+1), this yields √2 = 1 + 1·1/(1 + 2·3/(1 + 4·5/(1 + 6·7/(1 + …)))).

Problem IV announces the power-series version: s = x/α − x²/(αβ) + x³/(αβγ) − …. It is solved on the next page as Theorem VIII: x/s = α + αx/(β − x + βx/(γ − x + …)).
errors: No algebraic errors. The equivalence transformation is correct, and the convergents reproduce the partial sums (1/2, 1/8, …).

Euler does not remark that the series 1/2 − 3/8 + 15/48 − … converges only conditionally and very slowly (terms behave like 1/√(πn)). The resulting continued fraction for √2 therefore converges equally slowly and oscillates (convergents 7, 1.286, 5.09, … for √2+1). Its practical value is nil compared with the regular continued fraction [1;2,2,2,…]. This is a gap of commentary, not of logic.

ideas.what: Transformation of an alternating series with term ratios a/α, b/β, … into an equivalent continued fraction whose convergents are the partial sums (Theorem VII)
ideas.modern_name: Euler's continued fraction formula (equivalence of series and continued fractions)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Introductio in analysin infinitorum, 1748, ch. 18; also E593)
ideas.where_published: Introductio I, ch. XVIII; E593 (Opuscula analytica II, 1785)

ideas.what: Rescaling the partial numerators and denominators (multiplying the k-th fraction top and bottom by a constant)
ideas.where_published: Introductio ch. XVIII and many continued-fraction papers

ideas.what: Continued fraction √2 = 1 + 1/(1 + 2·3/(1 + 4·5/(1 + 6·7/(1+…)))), from the binomial series of (1+1)^{−1/2}
ideas.modern_name: non-regular continued fraction for √2; special case of the Euler/Gauss continued fraction for a binomial series
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this paper); a special case of general formulas in standard handbooks

ideas.what: Power-series version x/s = α + αx/(β − x + βx/(γ − x + …)) (Problem IV, Theorem VIII)
ideas.modern_name: Euler's continued fraction for a power series

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds a routine restatement of Euler's well-known series-to-continued-fraction formula and a worked example for √2. That example is an immediate special case of a published, classical formula. There is nothing unfinished or uncredited here.
